newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Catalans not seen derailing Spain budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Catalans not seen derailing Spain budget.

text.p: The Spanish government's Catalan allies turned up the pressure for concessions on Tuesday as talks for the key 1997 budget entered the final two weeks, but the administration said it sees no major obstacles to approval.

Catalonia's Convergencia i Unio (CiU) slapped down press reports that it had already given its crucial endorsement for a budget draft that makes or breaks Spain's chances of joining in the launch of Europe's single currency in 1999.
"There is as yet no agreement for support," a spokeswoman for the legislative group told Reuters. "The 'yes' won't be given until the final moment, until the vote in parliament."
Far from over, the talks were actually in a difficult period, a Catalonian leader told a Spanish radio station.
"The budget talks are really going through a tough time," said Josep Antoni Duran i Lleida. "There is one main issue, principally that of the financing of the health budget."
But a spokesman for the Economy Ministry played down any worries about its key ally's support.
"We are in a process of talks and we believe there won't be any more serious problems. It would be logical that there is support from CiU for the budget," the spokesman said.
The conservative government must present the budget draft to the legislature by the end of the month.

Although the CiU's 16 legislative seats could thwart the government's first budget and its European aspirations, leader and ally Jordi Pujol has vowed to support rigorous annual accounts that adhere to the EU's single currency requirements.
At issue for Catalonia is the repayment of 60 billion pesetas ($471 million) the central government owes the region for health care, of which the Catalans demand that 32 billion be paid back in 1997.
The Bank of America said in a brokers' note it expected the governing Popular Party (PP) to give ground on this issue.
"The PP will probably have to recognise and cover some of this debt to Catalonia," the Bank of America said.
The tussle had little impact on financial markets, where economists and traders assumed that the regional party would eventually lend its support.

"They (the Catalans) are pressing to get the best deal for Catalonia. But they are not going to be responsible for sinking the budget again," said Isabel Lasheras, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
The Catalans voted against the administration on the budget last autumn, prompting early elections that ousted the ruling Socialists after 13 years in power.

"I wouldn't pay very much attention to this. We've seen it all before (in the run-up to the general election). The Catalans are always going to try to get as much out of the central government as they can," said a stock market dealer at Banco Bilbao Vizcaya in Madrid. ($1=127.4 Peseta)
